title: Introduction
content:
Concepts RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation): retrieves relevant passages first (Retrieval), injects them into the prompt (Augmentation), and lets the model answer based strictly on those passages (Generation). Knowledge Base on DynamoDB: legal articles are stored as items in a DynamoDB table and queried by keywords. This approach is simple and fits within the AWS Free Tier, though it does not capture semantics like vector search. Serverless: Lambda, API Gateway, and DynamoDB scale automatically and bill by usage, making them suitable for low-budget projects. Groq API: an external inference service running a language model (qwen/qwen3.8-27b), called by Lambda over HTTPS. Problem and Objectives Employees need quick answers regarding personal data regulations (for example, using customer citizen ID / CCCD data to send marketing messages). Public chatbots may fabricate legal articles or citations. Objective: answers stay strictly grounded in the legal texts provided by the team, running on AWS at nearly zero cost.
Architecture Diagram & Data Flow Architecture and Data Flow Data flow:
Users open the website on S3, type a question into the chat box, and submit. index.html sends an HTTP POST over HTTPS to API Gateway. API Gateway checks CORS and forwards the payload to the Lambda function. Lambda queries the LegalArticles DynamoDB table to find legal articles relevant to the question (retrieve_legal_context function). DynamoDB returns matching legal articles to Lambda as legal context. Lambda assembles the complete prompt (system prompt + legal context + question) and calls the Groq API. Groq returns the answer text to Lambda. Lambda formats a standard JSON response (including error codes if any) and returns it to API Gateway. API Gateway returns the result and the chat box displays it. Lambda logs are written to Amazon CloudWatch throughout the process. Components Component AWS Service / Resource Prompt & RAG logic Lambda (Python) Knowledge Base DynamoDB – LegalArticles Backend API API Gateway + Lambda Frontend S3 static website – index.html Security & Operations CloudWatch, Budgets, IAM Implemented vs. Planned The system differs from the initial design in several areas. This table helps the workshop accurately reflect what is currently in place.

Answer based strictly on the provided legal articles; do not fabricate articles or citations. No basis in the database → state clearly.

Exploring aws amplify: Why is it a great choice for personal projects or students assignments? Whenever you work on a student assignment or build a personal project, you have probably experienced this scenario: finishing the user interface (Frontend) very quickly, only to spend a massive amount of time building the Backend, configuring the Database, integrating Sign-up/Sign-in flows, and deploying to a server.
To solve the challenge of complex infrastructure setup and help you focus entirely on application logic, AWS Amplify is a solution well worth considering.
What is AWS Amplify?
AWS Amplify is a set of tools and services that enables developers to rapidly build full-stack Web and Mobile applications on AWS infrastructure without needing deep expertise in Cloud or DevOps management.
Key Features
Authentication: Integrates Amazon Cognito with just a few CLI commands or simple configurations. It provides out-of-the-box sign-up, sign-in, password reset, and secure session management flows.
API & Database: Flexibly initializes GraphQL APIs (AWS AppSync) or REST APIs (API Gateway combined with DynamoDB). Data operations from the Frontend are optimized and seamlessly synchronized.
Automated Hosting & CI/CD: Connects directly to GitHub or GitLab. Every time you push new code (git push), the system automatically executes the Build and Deploy process.
Practical Experience Review
Pros:
Optimal deployment speed: Particularly well-suited for demo projects, course assignments, or MVP (Minimum Viable Product) builds.
Serverless architecture: Eliminates the cost and effort of maintaining or managing servers.
Cross-platform support: Integrates seamlessly with popular frameworks such as React, Next.js, Vue, Flutter, React Native, etc.
Cons:
As the application scales and requires deep infrastructure customization (such as custom VPC configurations or complex IAM permissions), modifying the underlying resources automatically provisioned by Amplify requires additional research and effort.
Summary AWS Amplify is an effective solution that streamlines the development workflow and brings your product to the Cloud reliably while saving significant time.

Summary Report: “ Talkshow “The Thinking Behind Building The Bot” ” Event Objectives This talkshow offered a practical perspective on AI Agents and AI-driven applications. Rather than focusing solely on AI technology itself, the session explored how developers approach real-world problems when building AI-powered bots. It also gave attendees a chance to learn from seasoned engineers and technical leaders, see how AI operates in enterprise settings, and gain clearer career insights in the tech industry. Speakers Thien Lu – Program Manager, First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) Truong Bui – Tech Lead, CMC Global Phong Pham – Program Manager, First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) Key Highlights Understanding AI Agents The session unpacked how AI Agents go beyond traditional chatbots to handle more complex, real-world tasks. Building an AI bot is more than wiring an app to a model; it requires understanding the underlying problem, user interaction patterns, and how the system processes and responds to information. Real-World Programming Problems Discussions bridged AI concepts with everyday software engineering scenarios, showing why user needs and business goals come before technical novelty. Effective AI solutions start with a well-defined problem and then identify where AI creates tangible user value. The Thinking Behind Building a Bot A standout takeaway was the structured questioning process before picking any tech stack:
What problem should the bot solve? Who are the end users? What information does the bot need? What actions or capabilities should it have? How should it respond across different scenarios? How should the system be architected for reliability in production? This shifted the mindset from simply “using AI” to architecting a complete solution around a concrete problem.
Enterprise Perspective Insights from CMC Global highlighted that enterprise AI systems must go beyond core functionality to address reliability, security, scalability, and measurable business value.
Career and Industry Insights The closing discussion with CMC Global representatives offered practical context on career paths, interviews, and core competencies expected of engineers working on AI-enabled software.
Key Takeaways Technical: AI Agents enable more capable workflows than standard chatbots; AI models must sit inside a cohesive application flow that accounts for reliability, security, scalability, and user needs. Problem-Solving Mindset: Start with the problem and business requirements before choosing AWS services or AI models, and break complex problems into smaller parts to simplify design and execution. Career: Building AI systems requires blending AI literacy with solid software engineering fundamentals, problem-solving, system design, and business alignment. Applying to Work These lessons apply directly to my FCAJ project focused on an AI assistant for enterprise legal and security information. Previously, the focus leaned toward mapping out AWS services such as Amazon Bedrock, Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, API Gateway, and DynamoDB. Following the event, defining the core problem comes first. Event Experience Learning from Speakers: Gained real-world perspectives from technical leaders and program managers experienced in delivering technology and AI initiatives. Real-World AI Development: Connected academic AI concepts with practical software engineering workflows rather than treating them purely as theory. Problem-Solving & Technical Thinking: Reinforced the habit of justifying technology choices against concrete requirements in the FCAJ project. Career Discussion: Built a clearer view of industry expectations, encouraging stronger technical skills alongside clear project communication, problem-solving, and teamwork. Core Lesson: A valuable AI application is defined not merely by model power, but by a clear problem, a sound workflow, reliable data, thoughtful system design, and real-world constraints—providing a stronger foundation for executing the FCAJ project ahead.

title: Proposal
content:
Legal RAG Platform: Automated Legal Advisory System for Decree 13/2023/ND-CP A Unified AWS Serverless Solution with LLM for Real-Time Legal Research and Analysis 1. Executive Summary The Legal RAG Platform is an automated advisory system that helps users and team members quickly look up and analyze complex Vietnamese legal regulations. It focuses on Decree 13/2023/ND-CP on personal data protection. The platform is built on a fully serverless architecture on AWS and uses a large language model (LLM) from the Groq API (qwen/qwen3.8-27b). Answers are grounded in the actual legal text, which reduces the risk of AI hallucination. The platform also keeps operating costs at $0 by staying within the AWS Free Tier.
2. Problem Statement The Problem Legal documents such as Decree 13/2023/ND-CP are long, dense, and difficult for non-experts to search manually. General-purpose AI tools, such as the free version of ChatGPT, often lack in-depth knowledge of Vietnamese law. They tend to give generic answers without an accurate legal basis. Building a self-hosted AI system is expensive in hardware and complex to operate. The Solution The platform uses an automated RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) pipeline. When a user submits a question, the system searches the database for the most relevant legal provisions and injects them into a System Prompt. The LLM then generates an answer that cites those provisions clearly.
Amazon DynamoDB stores the extracted legal provisions in the LegalArticles table. AWS Lambda handles the backend logic, and Amazon API Gateway exposes a stable API endpoint. Groq API with the qwen/qwen3.8-27b model generates clear, coherent answers. Amazon S3 Static Website hosts the web interface, where users interact through a chat window. Benefits and Return on Investment (ROI) High accuracy: Answers stay close to the provided legal text and are transparent and well-supported. Cost efficiency: The serverless design runs within the AWS Free Tier, with monthly costs close to $0. Scalability: The decoupled architecture makes it easy to add new legal documents, such as the Law on Network Information Security or the Law on Information Technology, to DynamoDB in the future. 3. Solution Architecture The system follows a serverless architecture that connects the frontend, backend, and external LLM in a closed loop.
AWS Services and Technologies Amazon S3 Static Website: Hosts and serves the static web interface (index.html, CSS, and JavaScript). Amazon API Gateway: Provides a public HTTP/REST API, handles CORS, and forwards client requests to Lambda. AWS Lambda (Python): Runs the RAG logic, queries DynamoDB, and calls the Groq API. Amazon DynamoDB (LegalArticles): Stores legal provisions and supports fast keyword-based lookup. Groq API (qwen/qwen3.8-27b): Generates and analyzes natural language based on the legal context provided. Component Design Frontend: Users open the website hosted on S3 and enter a question in the chat window. The browser sends an HTTP POST request containing the question over HTTPS to API Gateway. API Gateway: Receives the request, validates CORS settings, and forwards the payload to the Lambda function. Data Retrieval (DynamoDB): The retrieve_legal_context function searches the LegalArticles table for relevant provisions. For example, it can retrieve rules on handling violations involving citizen identity numbers (CCCD) and personal data under Decree 13. Augmentation and Generation (Groq API): Lambda combines the user’s question with the retrieved legal context into a System Prompt with strict constraints, which require answers to be based only on the provided context. It then calls the Groq API. Response Flow: Groq returns the result to Lambda. Lambda formats a standard JSON response and sends it back through API Gateway to display in the chat window. 4. Technical Implementation Implementation Phases
Phase 1, Prompt Design and RAG Mechanism: Write a System Prompt that defines the role of a legal expert and sets a context constraint that prohibits fabricated information. Phase 2, Backend and Database: Create the DynamoDB LegalArticles table. Write the Python code for AWS Lambda, including the retrieval function and the Groq API integration. Configure API Gateway, enable CORS headers, and implement standardized error handling. This covers codes 400 and 502/504, as well as code 429 when the Groq API rate limit is exceeded. Phase 3, Testing and Refinement: Send HTTP POST requests with curl and test directly in the web interface. Monitor logs in Amazon CloudWatch. 5. Timeline & Milestones Project Timeline
Research and Design: Define the legal scope (Decree 13/2023/ND-CP) and design the RAG data flow. Development and Deployment: Build the DynamoDB database, complete the Lambda function, and configure API Gateway. Integration and Testing: Connect the S3 static website to API Gateway, test the accuracy of answers from the Groq LLM, and refine error handling. 6. Budget Estimation Infrastructure Costs AWS Services: Amazon S3: Free within Free Tier limits. Amazon API Gateway: Free for the first 1 million requests per month. AWS Lambda: Free for up to 1 million requests per month. Amazon DynamoDB: Free within 25 GB of storage and 25 WCU and 25 RCU. Total AWS cost: $0.00 per month. Groq API: The project uses the free tier for the open-source model (qwen/qwen3.8-27b). Total project investment: VND 0 ($0).
7. Risk Assessment Risk Matrix API overload (Groq API rate limit, error 429): Implement error handling and display a clear, user-friendly message in the chat interface when the request limit is temporarily exceeded. Inaccurate AI answers (hallucination): Strengthen the System Prompt so the model uses only the legal context retrieved from DynamoDB and does not infer beyond that source. CORS errors in the browser: Configure full CORS headers (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, POST, OPTIONS) directly in API Gateway. 8. Expected Outcomes Technical Achievements: A complete serverless backend that scales automatically, runs reliably, and operates at $0 cost.
Practical Value: A standardized API gateway and an intuitive chat interface that enable fast, accurate lookup of the core provisions of Decree 13/2023/ND-CP. The platform supports both study and research.

title: Blog 2
content:
What should you keep in mind when starting with AWS to avoid any “nasty surprises” on your end-of-month bill? One of the most common situations for beginners exploring AWS is accidentally spinning up a test resource and forgetting to turn it off, only to receive an unexpected bill at the end of the month. Controlling costs not only gives you peace of mind while practicing, but is also a foundational skill in cloud infrastructure management.
Below are the essential setups and considerations to help you manage your budget effectively right from day one.
Set Up AWS Budgets & Billing Alerts This is the very first step you should take right after creating your AWS account.
Mechanism: Configure a safe budget threshold (for example, $5 or $10). When actual or forecasted costs exceed this threshold, the system automatically sends an email notification.
Benefit: Prevents background resources from running continuously without timely detection.
Use the AWS Free Tier Properly
The Free Tier provides many free resources, but it comes with specific conditions:
Time limits: For instance, EC2 offers 750 hours/month for t2.micro or t3.micro instances (depending on the Region). If you run two instances simultaneously and continuously, usage hours are counted twice and will quickly exceed the free quota. Storage limits: Services like S3 and EBS have strict limits on storage capacity and request counts. Always read the service terms carefully before provisioning. Clean Up Unused Resources
“Orphaned” or standalone resources are frequently the cause of hidden charges:
Stop or terminate EC2 instances: Shut down test servers whenever you are not actively working on them.
Watch out for Elastic IPs: An Elastic IP is only free while attached to a Running EC2 instance. If it is disassociated or attached to a Stopped instance, you will still be billed an hourly maintenance fee.
Delete Unattached EBS Volumes & Snapshots: When you terminate an EC2 instance, certain auto-created EBS volumes or snapshots may remain behind independently and continue incurring storage fees.
Track Usage in Detail with AWS Cost Explorer Visual tool: AWS Cost Explorer provides charts breaking down costs over time, by service, or by Tag. Regular checks: Making a habit of reviewing cost reports 1–2 times per week helps you quickly spot services consuming an abnormal share of your budget. Summary
Optimizing and controlling costs is an indispensable part of the Cloud Computing mindset. Setting up safe guardrails from the start allows you to comfortably learn and experiment with AWS services without worrying about unexpected bills. Link to the post on AWS Study Group

This topic helps build a broader view of how AI moves beyond simple question-and-answer interactions to participate in systems that help users complete more complex tasks.
Data Analytics The event emphasizes the foundational role of data in modern cloud applications. Data is an important launchpad for AI and enterprise applications; organizations need appropriate ways to collect, process, analyze, and leverage data before effectively harnessing AI technologies.
Cloud Migration The content on Cloud Migration shares how organizations move existing infrastructure and applications to the Cloud while balancing scalability, cost, reliability, and modernization. This process is not merely lifting and shifting a system from physical servers to AWS, but also a time to consider modernizing applications during migration.
Modern Application Development The program introduces modern approaches to building applications on the Cloud platform. Modern applications need to aim for scalability, flexibility, availability, and resource optimization — principles that are very helpful for learning AWS and choosing the right services for a project.
Industry Solutions Stories from organizations and businesses applying Cloud and AI in practice show that AWS technologies do not stop at technical experimentation, but directly solve operational problems across different industries.
Key Takeaways Cloud and AI are closely connected: Cloud computing builds the foundation for AI applications in compute capacity, data storage, networking, security, and elastic infrastructure, helping businesses build and deploy AI more effectively. Start from the business problem: Before choosing AWS services or AI technologies, it is necessary to clarify the problem to solve, target users, required data, system goals, as well as technical and business constraints. Modernization goes beyond migration: Cloud migration is an opportunity to upgrade applications through managed services, serverless technologies, modern architectures, and AI when appropriate, instead of keeping the old architecture in a new environment. Applying to the FCAJ Project Knowledge from AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi applies directly to the FCAJ project building an AI assistant for enterprise legal and security information. The event reinforces the principle of defining the business problem first before selecting AWS services.
For example, when an enterprise user enters a legal or security situation, the system will rely on the internal knowledge base to generate an appropriate response. From that requirement, a corresponding AWS architecture can be shaped:
Amazon S3 → store internal documents and knowledge sources Amazon Bedrock → provide AI capabilities and foundation models AWS Lambda → execute application logic Amazon API Gateway → provide APIs for the application Amazon DynamoDB → store application data and conversation history In addition, because organizational data can be sensitive, system design needs to emphasize security, scalability, and responsible use of enterprise data.
Event Experience Learning from AWS experts: Get updated on the Cloud and AI landscape directly from AWS experts and industry leaders, gaining multiple perspectives from technology and business to product development. Exploring current AI trends: Discussions around Agentic AI show that AI is shifting from a chatbot/Q&A tool to becoming a link in the overall application workflow. Understanding enterprise Cloud adoption: Practical insights from Techcombank and Katalon show that deploying Cloud and AI is also tied to business value, security, scalability, cost, and impact on existing systems. Most Important Lesson: Cloud and AI technologies should be viewed as tools for solving real-world problems rather than used simply because of novelty. This helps orient the FCAJ project more practically: grasp the problem and requirements first, then design the architecture and choose suitable AWS services.

Steps
Write a role definition statement (Vietnamese personal data law specialist). Require answers in Vietnamese and state the legal articles used. Add a disclaimer: preliminary answer, not official legal advice. Verification The model responds in the expected role and tone.
5.3.2 Setting Context Constraints Objective Force the model to answer based strictly on legal texts retrieved from the database.
Steps
Add strict rules: answer only based on the provided legal texts; do not fabricate or extrapolate outside the context. Add a fallback mechanism: if the provided texts are insufficient, clearly state that there is not enough legal basis. Test with out-of-scope questions (for example, questions about taxes). Verification Out-of-scope questions receive a “not enough legal basis” response instead of a fabricated answer.
5.3.3 Defining Input Data Structure Objective Decide how Lambda injects DynamoDB data into the outgoing prompt.
Steps
Format each retrieved legal article into a labeled block (article number + content). Place the legal context before the user’s question in the message. Limit the number and length of legal articles so they stay within the model’s rate and token limits. Verification The printed prompt contains all three parts in the right order.

content:
Event Report: “AWS Cloud Architecture, Software Factories, and Career Growth” Event Objectives The event offered a well-rounded look at modern cloud architecture, spotlighting serverless computing and asynchronous system design. Moving beyond pure theory, the sessions shared practical lessons from building “software factories” at enterprise scale. It also gave attendees a chance to learn from seasoned practitioners on preparing for a cloud career, closing the gap between university curricula and industry expectations, and navigating technical internships alongside open-source contributions. Speakers List Thinh Nguyen – SYL Solution Henry Duc Bui – CloudThinker Hung Tran – NAB Dao Luong – FCAJ Khang Duong – FCAJ Tuan Tran – FCAJ Key Highlights Building Software Factories at Scale The program opened with practical takeaways on running “software factories.” The discussion unpacked common bottlenecks teams encounter when scaling software delivery, emphasizing that operating at scale demands more than clean code—it requires standardized workflows, automation, and battle-tested practices from enterprise engineering teams.
Bridging the Education and Industry Gap The education-focused session highlighted what students should prepare before stepping into the cloud workforce. It underscored that academic foundations must go hand in hand with hands-on technical skills to align university training with real business demands.
Rethinking Serverless with AWS Lambda One of the standout technical deep dives explored AWS Lambda Web Functions, explaining how native HTTP support and 128-request multi-concurrency are reshaping serverless compute. The session demonstrated how removing adapter overhead and leveraging Active CPU Billing maximize cost efficiency, backed by live performance benchmarks comparing Serverless against Docker workloads on EC2 and ECS.
Building Asynchronous Systems with Amazon SQS The Amazon SQS session tied architectural theory to practical system design, illustrating why modern applications lean on asynchronous processing to decouple services and scale smoothly. Speakers shared concrete design patterns and actionable tips for integrating SQS in production workloads.
Career Growth: Internships and Open Source The second half of the event centered on career progression. Hearing firsthand about a 3-month AWS internship—and how cloud services were applied to real projects—provided practical guidance. In addition, the open-source session walked through making a first contribution from scratch, building a consistent habit, and using open-source work to accelerate technical growth.
Key Takeaways Technical Perspective: Serverless architecture is advancing rapidly, with AWS Lambda features like multi-concurrency and Active CPU Billing delivering major gains in performance and cost efficiency. Meanwhile, scalable cloud systems depend on decoupled designs powered by tools like Amazon SQS, and building at scale relies on standardized “software factory” practices rather than isolated coding. System Design Mindset: The core architectural takeaway was choosing the right compute and messaging model up front. Before deploying an API or background job, developers should decide whether a workload belongs in a synchronous path (optimized Lambda functions) or an asynchronous flow (decoupled via SQS queues) to prevent bottlenecks and maintain reliability. Career Perspective: Breaking into the cloud industry takes proactive preparation. While technical proficiency is essential, hands-on experience—built through internships, practical AWS projects, and steady open-source contributions—is what sets candidates apart. Applying to the FCAJ Project Insights from this event translate directly into my FCAJ project, where I am developing an AWS Serverless Legal RAG Assistant.
Prior to attending, I had already provisioned the core stack using Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, API Gateway, DynamoDB, and a React frontend hosted on S3. However, the Lambda and SQS sessions sparked concrete ideas to refine the architecture:
Applying AWS Lambda Optimizations: My legal-ai-chat-lambda function currently processes incoming requests from API Gateway. Understanding multi-concurrency and Active CPU Billing helps me tune execution times and keep costs predictable when multiple users query the assistant concurrently. Applying Amazon SQS for Document Processing: Currently, legal documents land in my fcaj-raw-docs S3 bucket before being chunked. The SQS session inspired decoupling this ingestion pipeline by placing an Amazon SQS queue between S3 and the processing service. Handling document ingestion asynchronously ensures the system can absorb large batches of legal files gracefully without throttling or failing. This event shifted my focus from simply “getting the API to work” to “architecting a resilient, decoupled, and cost-effective serverless system.”
Event Experience Learning from Experienced Speakers: Hearing directly from engineers who have built large-scale production systems clarified how services like Lambda and SQS are applied in enterprise settings beyond introductory tutorials. Understanding Real-World Architecture: Rather than merely listing service features, live benchmarks and design patterns demonstrated why specific architectural choices are made to solve scalability and cost challenges in production. Career Motivation: The internship and open-source talks motivated me to look beyond my FCAJ project, start building a public contribution portfolio, and strengthen my collaboration skills for industry work. Most Important Lesson Building dependable cloud software requires pairing efficient compute (Lambda) with resilient messaging (SQS). A well-rounded cloud engineer must master not only technical implementation, but also a continuous learning habit grounded in real-world projects and open-source collaboration. This mindset will guide me as I refine my Legal RAG Assistant and grow my career.

title: Blog 3
content:
Building a simple, secure static website with S3 + cloudfront + route 53 Once you finish building a static website (plain HTML/CSS/JS or build artifacts from React, Vue, Next.js), the next challenge is choosing a solution to store and distribute it over the internet. Common goals include optimized cost, fast access speed, secure HTTPS support, and zero server management overhead. The trio of Amazon S3 + Amazon CloudFront + Route 53 is a standardized architecture that solves this problem cleanly and efficiently.
Solution Architecture & Implementation Steps
Step 1: Store Files with Amazon S3 Create an S3 Bucket to hold all built static web source files.
Configure the S3 Bucket Policy and set appropriate access permissions.
Enable Static website hosting to configure default entry documents (for example, index.html and 404.html).
Step 2: Accelerate & Secure with Amazon CloudFront (CDN)
Create a CloudFront Distribution and point the Origin to the newly created S3 Bucket. Acceleration: Web content is cached at Edge Locations globally, minimizing latency for users. Security: Integrate a free SSL/TLS certificate from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to enable HTTPS. At the same time, configure OAC (Origin Access Control) to block direct external access to the S3 Bucket and only allow traffic routed through CloudFront. Step 3: Route Custom Domains with Amazon Route 53
Create a Hosted Zone for your personal domain in Route 53. Configure an A Record (Alias type) to point your root domain or subdomain to the CloudFront Distribution address. Technical Value & Key Takeaways
Cost optimization: A Serverless architecture incurs zero cost for maintaining servers (Nginx/Apache). For low traffic or personal projects, monthly costs are nearly zero.
Scalability: CloudFront’s CDN network automatically handles traffic spikes without requiring infrastructure upgrades.
Simplified operations: No need to worry about OS patching or periodic SSL certificate renewals. Summary
This is one of the classic yet essential hands-on exercises that helps you master combining foundational AWS services to build a complete, secure, and industry-standard system.

title: Phase 2 – Backend: From Database to Lambda & API
content:
Overview Item Details Purpose Serverless backend that retrieves legal articles, calls the LLM, and provides a stable API. AWS Services DynamoDB, Lambda, API Gateway, CloudWatch Inputs HTTP POST containing the user’s question Outputs Standard JSON containing the answer or an error code Dependencies Prompt from Phase 1; Groq API key 5.4.1 Building the Knowledge Base on DynamoDB Objective Store legal articles in a table that Lambda can query.
Steps
Create the LegalArticles DynamoDB table
In the AWS Management Console, type DynamoDB in the search bar and press Enter.
In the left menu, select Tables, then select Create table. Table details:
Table name: name the table LegalArticles. Length is 3–255 characters, containing only letters, numbers, underscores (_), hyphens (-), and periods (.). Partition key: enter id, type String. This is the primary key used to identify each legal article. DynamoDB hashes this value to determine where to store and find items. Sort key (optional): leave blank since the table only needs a single key, id. Keep default settings and select Create table. After a few seconds, the LegalArticles table transitions to Active. Subsequent steps add articles from Decree 13/2023/ND-CP into this table.
Prepare the IAM Role for Lambda
In the AWS Management Console, type IAM in the search bar and press Enter. On the IAM Dashboard:
Security recommendations shows the account meets two security recommendations: MFA is enabled on the root user, and the root user has no active access keys. This follows best practice: enable MFA on root and work via an IAM user. IAM resources summarizes existing resources: 1 user group, 4 users, 13 roles, 20 policies, and 0 identity providers. The left menu includes Roles, Policies, IAM users, etc. We will use Roles to create a role for Lambda. In the left menu, select Roles.
The Roles list page displays the account’s roles (13). A role is an identity with specific permissions and short-term credentials that trusted entities (such as Lambda) can assume.
Select Create role on the right to create a new role. When creating the role, configure as follows:
Trusted entity type: select AWS service, Use case: select Lambda. Permissions: attach the managed policy AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole so Lambda can write logs to CloudWatch, and add a policy allowing read access to the LegalArticles table (granting only least-privilege permissions needed). Role name: enter a descriptive name, for example legal-ai-chat-role. Select Create role. (Retrieving articles from DynamoDB – retrieve_legal_context) 5.4.2 Programming the AWS Lambda Function (RAG Logic & Groq API) Objective Retrieve legal context and generate answers within a single Python function.
Steps
Create the Lambda function
In the AWS Management Console, type Lambda in the search bar and press Enter.
The Functions page lists Lambda functions in the current region. Select Create function on the right to create a new function.
On the Create function page, select Author from scratch: Function name: name it legal-ai-chat-lambda. Length is 1–64 characters, no spaces, containing only letters, numbers, hyphens (-), and underscores (_). Runtime: select Python 3.12 (the language for writing the function; the console editor supports Node.js, Python, and Ruby). Permissions: by default, Lambda creates an execution role with only CloudWatch Logs write permissions. Because our function also needs to read DynamoDB, we will use an existing role in the next step. Attach the created Execution Role
Scroll down to Additional settings and toggle on Custom execution role. Keep other options such as ARM64 architecture, Function URL, VPC, and Durable execution turned off.
When Custom execution role is enabled, the Configure custom execution role panel appears on the right. Open the Execution role dropdown to select an existing role:
Execution role: select legal-ai-chat-role (the role created in the previous step). To inspect the role’s permissions, select View role details in IAM. Select Save. Check Networking and Security & governance: leave Function URL, VPC, Tenant isolation mode, Code signing, Encryption with AWS KMS, and Tags at their defaults (off). We will use API Gateway instead of a Function URL. Note: settings with special icons cannot be added or removed after function creation; remaining settings can be changed later.
Select Create function. A confirmation message indicates the function was created successfully. Program the Lambda function (lambda_function.py) After pasting the code into lambda_function.py, select Deploy to save and apply the code. The green banner Successfully updated the function “legal-ai-chat-lambda” indicates the code is updated. If you do not click Deploy, Lambda continues running the old code. Add the GROQ_API_KEY environment variable
The code reads the key from the GROQ_API_KEY environment variable so we do not hardcode keys directly in the source code. Select the Configuration tab, then select Environment variables in the left menu. Environment variables (0) is empty → select Edit to add a new variable. On the Edit environment variables page, select Add environment variable and enter: Key: GROQ_API_KEY Value: paste the gsk_... API key copied when creating the key on Groq. Select Save. After saving, the system displays Successfully updated the function. GROQ_API_KEY is now attached to the function; if missing, the function returns error 500 (“Thiếu cấu hình GROQ_API_KEY trên hệ thống”) as written in the code. Increase the function Timeout
Under the Configuration tab, select General configuration. By default, the function has 128 MB Memory, 512 MB Ephemeral storage, and a 3 second Timeout. A 3-second timeout is too short because the function must query DynamoDB, call the Groq API, and wait for the model to generate a response. If it times out, Lambda terminates execution and the client receives an error. Select Edit to update: Timeout: set to 0 min 30 sec. Execution role: keep legal-ai-chat-role. Memory: keep 128 MB, which is sufficient for this workshop. Scroll to the bottom of the page and select Save. (Processing flow inside the Lambda function) 5.4.3 Configuring API Gateway & Standardizing Error Handling Objective Expose the Lambda function through a public HTTPS endpoint that browsers are allowed to call.
Steps
Create an API (HTTP or REST) with a POST route pointing to the Lambda function. Configure CORS: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, with POST and OPTIONS methods. Build an error-handling layer in Lambda returning the codes in the table below. Deploy the stage and record the API invocation URL. Code When Meaning for Client 400 Invalid request data Fix the request 429 Groq API rate limit reached Wait and retry 502 / 504 System or AI error Retry later Configuring API Gateway for the Lambda Function Create an HTTP API
In the AWS Management Console, type API Gateway in the search bar and press Enter. API Gateway is a fully managed service for creating, publishing, monitoring, and securing APIs at any scale; here it acts as the public HTTPS gateway for the S3 website to call the Lambda function. Select Create an API in the Get started box. On the Choose an API type page, find the HTTP API card and select Build. HTTP APIs offer low latency, low cost, built-in CORS support, and integration with Lambda or HTTP backends—sufficient and cheaper than REST APIs for this workshop.
Step 1: Configure API
Under API details: API name: name it LegalChatAPI. IP address type: keep IPv4. Integrations: select Add integration to choose the backend service the API will call. Under Integrations: Choose the Lambda integration type. AWS Region: select the Lambda function’s region. Lambda function: select legal-ai-chat-lambda. Version: keep 2.0 (HTTP API payload format version 2.0). Select Next. Step 2: Configure routes
A route consists of two parts: Method (HTTP method) and Resource path. Method: POST Resource path: enter /chat. Integration target: select legal-ai-chat-lambda. Select Next. Step 3: Define stages
A Stage is a deployment environment for the API (for example dev, prod). By default, the console creates the $default stage. Auto-deploy: enabled, meaning changes are automatically deployed to this stage. Keep defaults and select Next. Step 4: Review and create
Review the full configuration: API name: LegalChatAPI, IPv4. Integrations: legal-ai-chat-lambda (Lambda). Routes: ANY /chat → legal-ai-chat-lambda. Stages: $default (Auto-deploy: enabled). Select Create. Once created, Successfully created API LegalChatAPI appears. Configure CORS CORS allows a website on one domain (the S3 website) to call an API on another domain (API Gateway). Without it, browsers block the request.
In the left menu under Develop, select CORS. Currently all fields show No Origins/Headers/Methods are allowed → select Configure. Enter the values: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: enter * and select Add (allows any origin). Access-Control-Allow-Headers: enter content-type and select Add. Access-Control-Allow-Methods: select POST and OPTIONS. Access-Control-Max-Age: set to 0. Allow-Credentials: set to NO. Select Save. Create stage and deploy
Create stage v1. Stage details displays the Invoke URL in the format https://<api-id>.execute-api.<region>[.amazonaws.com/v1](https://.amazonaws.com/v1). This is the base URL to call the API. Automatic Deployment for stage v1 is Disabled, so you must click Deploy manually whenever configuration changes. Select Deploy and choose stage v1. The message Successfully created deployment for LegalChatAPI. This deployment is active for v1 confirms deployment. The full URL to invoke the function is Invoke URL + route: https://<api-id>.execute-api.<region>[.amazonaws.com/v1/chat](https://.amazonaws.com/v1/chat) 5.4.4 Testing the Backend Objective Prove the backend works before connecting the frontend.
Steps
Send a POST request using curl with a sample question. Open CloudWatch Logs and inspect response time, returned data, and JSON structure. Test error cases: empty question (400) and, if possible, rate-limit exceeded (429). curl -X POST "<API_URL>" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"question": "Dùng CCCD để trao đổi mua bán có được không.?"}' Verification curl returns a grounded answer and logs show the complete execution flow.

title: Frontend – S3 Static Website
content:
Overview Item Details Purpose Chat page for users to ask questions and read answers. AWS Services Amazon S3 (static website hosting) Inputs User question Outputs Answer displayed in the chat box Dependencies Backend API URL 5.5.1 Building the Chat Interface (index.html) Objective A single static page calling the backend using fetch.

Display clear messages for errors (400, 429, 502/504). Recommendation: add a disclaimer showing that answers are preliminary, not legal advice. Enable static website hosting

Verification The endpoint [http://ai-legal-assistant-frontend-hau.s3-website-ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com/](http://ai-legal-assistant-frontend-hau.s3-website-ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com/) loads the page.
5.5.3 Connecting the API and End-to-End Testing Objective Have the deployed page call the live backend.
Steps
Set the API URL in index.html and re-upload it. Open the website and ask a sample question. Open the browser console and verify there are no CORS errors. Check the request in CloudWatch Logs. Console Walkthrough Details
1: Properties tab of the bucket, view Region, ARN, and creation date. 2: Static website hosting is Disabled, select Edit. 3: Enable Static website hosting, select Host a static website, and set Index document to index.html. title: Workshop
content:
Overview AI Legal & Security Assistant is a preliminary legal advisory assistant for enterprises, focusing on Decree 13/2023/ND-CP (personal data protection). Users enter a question or a real-world scenario; the system retrieves relevant legal articles from the database, and then a large language model analyzes the question based strictly on those articles.
The system is not a lawyer and does not provide official legal conclusions. If the database lacks legal basis, the system must clearly state so.
The system is built on a serverless architecture with the following components:
Frontend – static website (index.html) hosted on Amazon S3 (static website hosting) API Gateway – Amazon API Gateway (CORS and error standardization) Backend – AWS Lambda (Python): retrieves legal articles and calls the LLM Knowledge Base – Amazon DynamoDB (LegalArticles table) LLM – Groq API (qwen/qwen3.8-27b), an external service outside AWS Monitoring – Amazon CloudWatch Contents 5.1 Introduction 5.2 Preparation 5.3 Phase 1 – Prompt Setup & RAG Mechanism 5.4 Phase 2 – Backend: From Database to Lambda & API 5.5 Frontend – S3 Static Website 5.6 Security & Operations 5.7 Final Outcomes and Future Directions 5.8 Resource Cleanup

title: Security & Operations
content:
Overview Item Details Purpose Understand current security posture, operational and cost monitoring, and plan improvements. AWS Services CloudWatch, AWS Budgets, IAM 5.6.1 Current Security Posture Area Current State Risk Recommendation API Gateway Rate/burst limits configured on stage v1 Anyone with the URL can call it and exhaust Groq quota Throttling + usage plan / API key; Cognito later CORS Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * Any website can call the API from a browser Restrict to the S3 site origin after the demo Groq API key Lambda environment variable Exposed if committed or shown in screenshots Move to SSM Parameter Store (SecureString); rotate key if leaked S3 website Public read, HTTP only Traffic is unencrypted Place CloudFront in front for HTTPS if needed Data sent to Groq Questions leave AWS Real customer data could leave the account Use sample questions only; review Groq data policy; consider Bedrock CloudWatch Lambda logging enabled Logs may contain user questions Set retention period (7–14 days); avoid logging sensitive data 5.6.2 Monitoring and Cost Control Objective Detect errors and cost anomalies early.
Steps
Set log retention for the Lambda log group. Create an alarm for Lambda errors (optional). Regularly check the Free Tier usage page under Billing and keep the Budget alert from Section 5.2 active. Console Walkthrough Details
1: CloudWatch overview page, open Logs to view Lambda logs. 2: Log groups list, the Lambda function’s log group created automatically by Lambda. 3: Log streams list, each stream records function requests along with the latest log timestamp. Verification Test requests appear in the logs; the Budget alert is active.
5.6.3 Security Hardening Roadmap Steps
Add throttling and a usage plan to the API to protect Groq quota (high priority, no frontend changes required). Move the Groq key to SSM Parameter Store and grant Lambda permission to read only that specific parameter. Restrict CORS to the website’s origin. Add Cognito sign-in if the system moves beyond demo mode. Testing: call the API at high rate to confirm throttling; test prompt injection questions; scan the repository for secrets. Configuring Throttling on API Gateway
1: Stage Throttling page, showing currently applied limits: Stage: select the stage to limit in the top-right corner (screenshot shows $default). Each stage has its own throttling configuration.
Selected route throttling: per-route limits (overrides default). Currently empty because no route is selected.
Default route throttling: limits applied to all routes in the stage. Currently Burst limit and Rate limit both show Not configured, meaning no limit is set.
Account throttling: account-wide ceiling in the region (Burst 5000, Rate 10000), shared across all APIs. This is a system-level limit and is not edited here. Select Edit under Default route throttling.
2: Set Burst limit = 2 and Rate limit = 5 for the default route: Rate limit: 5, maximum average requests per second. Burst limit: 2, maximum concurrent requests handled during a burst. Select Save, then select Deploy to apply. Requests exceeding the limit receive 429 Too Many Requests from API Gateway before reaching Lambda and Groq.

title: Sharing and Feedback
content:
Overall Evaluation Work Environment
The FCAJ environment is friendly and open. I can ask questions anytime—within my team as well as with mentors—and usually get responses fairly quickly. The combination of guided learning and self-paced hands-on practice helps me manage my schedule proactively. One area for improvement would be organizing a few more cross-team networking sessions so everyone can get to know each other better.
Support from Mentors / Admin Team
Mentors give concrete feedback on our Proposal and Workshop, pointing out areas that need adjustment such as architecture or cost estimation. I really appreciate that mentors let the team try and debug on our own first before suggesting a direction. The admin team provides clear, timely updates on schedules, events, and submission guidelines, helping me stay on top of each week’s requirements.
Alignment Between Work and Academic Major
The work aligns well with my university background in programming, databases, and networking. In addition, I was exposed to new areas: AWS services, serverless architecture, and working with an LLM inside a real application. This made the gap between theoretical knowledge and practical implementation much clearer.
Learning Opportunities & Skill Development
I learned how to select and combine AWS services while weighing cost, security, and operability. I also gained skills in reading logs to troubleshoot issues, testing APIs, writing technical documentation, and collaborating in a team. Talkshows, Cloud Day, and Fireside Chats helped broaden my perspective on career paths in the industry.
Culture & Team Spirit
Everyone respects one another, working seriously without unnecessary pressure. When tricky bugs come up, teammates are willing to sit down and debug together rather than leaving one person to handle it alone. I feel like a genuine part of the team rather than someone just executing assigned tasks.
Intern Policies / Benefits
I had flexible learning conditions and could join high-value program events and sharing sessions. AWS Free Tier resources and cost-control guides were also very helpful for newcomers.
Additional Questions What are you most satisfied with during your internship? I am most satisfied with building a working product end-to-end on my own—from choosing the architecture and writing the backend to testing and cleaning up resources. Previously, I had only worked on standalone labs. What do you think the program should improve for future interns? There should be additional guides or short sessions on AWS cost management and resource naming/organization right from the start. I would also like a few mid-term review sessions so teams can verify early whether they are on the right track. If recommending to friends, would you advise them to intern here? Why? Yes. The program gives you hands-on AWS experience on a real project, with mentors guiding you and a team building alongside you. The main requirement is being proactive in learning and dedicating consistent time each week. Suggestions & Expectations Suggestions to improve the experience: Share strong Proposal and Workshop examples from previous cohorts earlier, and hold a few small-group technical Q&A sessions. Would you like to continue with the program in the future? Yes, I would like to dive deeper into security and infrastructure on AWS. Other feedback: Thank you to all the mentors, the admin team, and my teammates for the support throughout this journey. I learned much more than I initially expected.

title: Final Outcomes and Future Directions
content: Outcomes A complete, auto-scaling serverless backend that, as noted by the team, costs $0 within the AWS Free Tier. A working RAG pipeline: each request looks up legal articles from DynamoDB and pairs them with the LLM to produce grounded answers. A stable API endpoint ready for the static website and for team members to test. Known Limitations Keyword lookup may miss relevant legal articles. Responses are plain text; there is no structured risk level yet. The LLM runs outside AWS and the API has no authentication yet. Future Directions Structured responses with risk level (Low / Medium / High / Insufficient evidence), articles, evidence, and sources. Human-confirmed incident reporting with email alerts via Amazon SNS (summary only, no sensitive data). Conversation history in DynamoDB with TTL. Evaluate Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock Knowledge Bases to keep all data within AWS (check current pricing and supported regions first).
